words.definition: Able to express thoughts and feelings clearly, fluently, and coherently in words.
words.example: Even under pressure, she stayed articulate, answering every question in crisp, complete sentences.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'articulus' (a joint) — you join your words together neatly, like well-fitted joints.

words.definition: Speaking or writing in a fluent, vivid, and deeply persuasive way that moves people.
words.example: His eloquent tribute at the funeral left the entire room in tears.
words.mnemonic: Hidden inside is Latin 'loqui' (to speak); think of words that 'quench' an audience's thirst for beauty.

words.definition: Using far more words than necessary, so the real meaning gets buried.
words.example: The manual was so verbose that finding one simple instruction took twenty minutes.
words.mnemonic: 'Verb-ose' — overflowing with verbs and words; Latin 'verbum' means 'word'.

words.definition: Talking readily, rapidly, and at great length, often without pausing.
words.example: A few glasses of wine made the usually shy accountant voluble, and he chattered all night.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'volume' — the volume of talk never turns off; root 'volvere' (to roll) as words roll out.

words.definition: Tediously long and drawn-out, stretching a small point far past patience.
words.example: The professor's prolix lectures could stretch a five-minute idea across a full hour.
words.mnemonic: 'Pro-lix' echoes 'pro-long'; from pro- (forth) + liquere (to flow) — words that flow on and on.

words.definition: Brief and to the point, using very few words, sometimes bordering on rude.
words.example: Her only reply to the long email was a terse 'No.'
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'curse' — a one-word curse is short, sharp, and clipped.

words.definition: Expressed clearly and briefly, with no wasted words at all.
words.example: The CEO's succinct summary fit the entire strategy onto a single index card.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'suck it in' — suck in the extra words; Latin 'succingere' means to gird tightly.

words.definition: Giving a lot of information clearly and completely in only a few words.
words.example: Keep the abstract concise: three sentences that capture the whole paper.
words.mnemonic: Like 'precise scissors' — root 'caedere' (to cut) — cut away every excess word.

words.definition: Rudely brief and abrupt in speech or manner, offering nothing extra.
words.example: 'Fine,' he said with a curt nod, then walked off without another word.
words.mnemonic: Short for 'curtailed' — a curt reply is speech cut short.

words.definition: Abrupt and short in manner, bordering on rude or dismissive.
words.example: The nurse's brusque manner softened once she saw how frightened the child was.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'brush' — he brushes you off quickly and roughly; from Italian 'brusco' (sharp, tart).

words.definition: Saying exactly what you think plainly, without any attempt to soften it.
words.example: To be blunt, your business plan has no realistic chance of making money.
words.mnemonic: A blunt knife has no fine edge — blunt speech has no soft, polished edges either.

words.definition: Honest, open, and straightforward, even about awkward or unflattering truths.
words.example: In a candid interview, the actor admitted he'd nearly quit the film halfway through.
words.mnemonic: Think 'Candid Camera' — it catches your honest, unguarded self; Latin 'candidus' means pure white.

words.definition: Speaking smoothly and easily but without sincerity or genuine thought.
words.example: His glib assurances that 'everything's handled' fooled no one who knew the details.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'glide' — words that glide out too smoothly and slickly to be trusted.

words.definition: Able to speak or write smoothly, easily, and without hesitation.
words.example: After a year in Madrid she became fluent, chatting with locals as if born there.
words.mnemonic: Root 'fluere' (to flow) — speech pours out like a smooth, flowing fluid.

words.definition: The art of using language skillfully to persuade or impress an audience.
words.example: The senator's speech was full of soaring rhetoric but offered no concrete plan.
words.mnemonic: From Greek 'rhetor' (public speaker) — picture a red-hot orator working the crowd.

words.definition: The art of making formal, persuasive public speeches.
words.example: Her closing argument was a piece of pure oratory that left the jury spellbound.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'ora' (to speak) + tory — think of a grand speaker who turns speech into an art.

words.definition: The skill of speaking or writing fluently and persuasively.
words.example: He accepted the award with such eloquence that even his rivals applauded.
words.mnemonic: e-LOQU- from Latin 'loqui' (to speak) — the same root hiding in 'ventriloquist,' one who speaks well.

words.definition: A formal discussion of a topic, spoken or written.
words.example: The professor's evening lecture became a wide-ranging discourse on the ethics of memory.
words.mnemonic: dis- (apart) + course — ideas running their full 'course' out loud from one mind to many.

words.definition: A long speech delivered by a single speaker.
words.example: The actor held the stage alone for ten minutes, his monologue building toward a whispered confession.
words.mnemonic: mono (one) + logue (speech) — one voice, no reply.

words.definition: The act of speaking one's thoughts aloud while alone.
words.example: Hamlet's famous soliloquy reveals a mind wrestling with itself in an empty hall.
words.mnemonic: soli (alone) + loqui (speak) — a 'solo' talk with no one else on stage.

words.definition: A formal or high-level conversation between two or more people.
words.example: The two envoys withdrew for a private colloquy before the treaty was signed.
words.mnemonic: col- (together) + loqui (speak) — people 'co-located' and speaking together.

words.definition: The skill of clear, expressive pronunciation in public speaking.
words.example: Years of elocution lessons had erased every trace of her childhood mumble.
words.mnemonic: e-LOCU (speak out) — imagine you 'lock you' each word into crisp shape before releasing it.

words.definition: The choice of words and clarity of pronunciation in speech.
words.example: The newscaster's crisp diction made every syllable easy to follow.
words.mnemonic: Same 'dict' (to say) root as dictionary — how well you say and select your words.

words.definition: To pronounce words clearly and distinctly.
words.example: Please enunciate when you leave a voicemail, or I can't tell your name from noise.
words.mnemonic: e-NUNCI — picture a stern nun making each child say every word crisply, like a papal 'nuncio' announcing news.

words.definition: To speak or recite formally and with dramatic emphasis.
words.example: He climbed onto the crate to declaim against the new tax to the gathering crowd.
words.mnemonic: de + claim — to loudly 'claim' your point before a whole crowd.

words.definition: To speak or write about a subject at great length or detail.
words.example: Ask him about trains and he will expatiate happily until your coffee goes cold.
words.mnemonic: ex + 'spatium' (space) — you spread out across a wide open 'space' of words.

words.definition: To express opinions in a pompous, dogmatic way, as if never wrong.
words.example: At every dinner he would pontificate about wine while everyone else quietly refilled their glasses.
words.mnemonic: pontiff (the Pope) — talk as if you spoke from the papal throne, grandly and infallibly.

words.definition: To explain something systematically and in careful detail.
words.example: The mechanic paused to expound exactly why the old design kept failing.
words.mnemonic: ex + pound — you 'pound out' every point of an idea until it's fully laid open.

words.definition: To make something clear by explaining it thoroughly.
words.example: A single well-drawn diagram can elucidate what three pages of text left murky.
words.mnemonic: e-LUCID — from 'lucid' (clear light) — to shine light onto a dark idea.

words.definition: To analyze and clarify the meaning of something in detail.
words.example: The seminar spent an hour helping students explicate a single dense stanza.
words.mnemonic: ex + 'plic' (fold) — to 'unfold' a tangled text; the same fold hiding in 'explicit.'

words.definition: To describe or draw the exact boundaries or details of something.
words.example: The contract carefully delineates each partner's rights and responsibilities.
words.mnemonic: de-LINE-ate has 'line' in it: you draw the lines that mark something out.

words.definition: To give a faint or partial outline of something, or hint at what is to come.
words.example: Her opening remarks adumbrated the reforms she would announce in full a month later.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'umbra' (shadow): you cast only a shadow of the full picture.

words.definition: To mention something in an indirect or passing way.
words.example: She never named him, but everyone knew whom she was alluding to.
words.mnemonic: Holds 'lud' from Latin 'ludere' (to play): you playfully point at a topic rather than say it outright.

words.definition: To hint at something bad in a sly, indirect way.
words.example: He insinuated that the manager had been cooking the books, without ever saying it outright.
words.mnemonic: Hides 'sinu-' like sinuous: a snake winding its way in to plant a hidden idea.

words.definition: To make something known quietly or by subtle hint.
words.example: By glancing pointedly at the clock, she intimated that the meeting should end.
words.mnemonic: An 'intimate' friend knows your secrets, so to intimate is to share a hint privately.

words.definition: To bring up a topic for the first time, often a difficult one.
words.example: I finally broached the subject of a raise with my boss over lunch.
words.mnemonic: Like tapping a 'broach' into a barrel: you pierce the silence to let a touchy topic out.

words.definition: To wander away from the main subject while speaking or writing.
words.example: The professor kept digressing into stories about his cat instead of finishing the lecture.
words.mnemonic: di- (away) + -gress (step, as in progress): you step away from the point.

words.definition: To talk on and on in a wandering, aimless way.
words.example: Grandpa rambled for an hour about the old days before we could steer him back.
words.mnemonic: Picture a rambler hiking with no fixed trail; your words wander just like the walk.

words.definition: To chatter in a silly, trivial, childish way.
words.example: The toddlers prattled happily about their imaginary friends all through dinner.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'prat' (a fool) plus 'tattle': foolish, trivial tattling.

words.definition: To talk quickly in a way that makes little or no sense.
words.example: The feverish patient babbled about clocks melting off the wall.
words.mnemonic: Think of the Tower of Babel: confused speech that nobody could understand.

words.definition: To talk at length in a foolish, long-winded way.
words.example: The candidate blathered on about values without ever answering the actual question.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'lather': words foaming up like empty suds, all bubbles and no substance.

words.definition: To speak fast and in a way that is hard to understand.
words.example: The excited tourists jabbered in a language I couldn't quite place.
words.mnemonic: 'jab' + -er: words jabbing out fast, like a flurry of quick punches (think Jabberwocky nonsense).

words.definition: To speak in a dull, monotonous voice that goes on and on.
words.example: The lecturer droned until half the class had quietly fallen asleep.
words.mnemonic: Picture a drone aircraft's steady hum or a bee's flat buzz: monotone and endless.

words.definition: To speak in a low, unclear voice, usually while grumbling.
words.example: He muttered a curse under his breath as he stubbed his toe on the door.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like a 'mutt' growling: a low grumble you can barely make out.

words.definition: To speak so quietly and unclearly that words are hard to catch.
words.example: The shy student mumbled his answer into his collar, and no one heard it.
words.mnemonic: Imagine a mouth full of marbles: the sounds come out soft and blurred.

words.definition: To say something in a low, soft, unclear voice.
words.example: She leaned close and murmured a secret so the others at the table wouldn't hear.
words.mnemonic: The word itself hums — 'mmm-mmm' — the low, blurred sound of quiet talking.

words.definition: To speak using only breath, so the sound barely carries.
words.example: He whispered the answer into my ear so the teacher wouldn't catch us.
words.mnemonic: Hidden inside is a 'hiss' — the breathy, airy sound of speaking without your voice.

words.definition: To speak with hesitant breaks and repeated sounds, often from nerves.
words.example: Put on the spot, he stammered through his apology, unable to finish a single sentence.
words.mnemonic: A 'stalled hammer' that keeps striking the same spot before it moves on.

words.definition: To involuntarily repeat the first sounds of words while trying to speak.
words.example: The nervous boy stuttered on the letter 'p' every time he tried to say 'please'.
words.mnemonic: The doubled 't-t' in the middle of the spelling mimics the repeated sound.

words.definition: To speak slowly, stretching out the vowel sounds.
words.example: The old rancher greeted us in a lazy Texan drawl that stretched every word to twice its length.
words.mnemonic: You 'draw' your words out long, like pulling taffy — drawl.

words.definition: To recite words in a slow, even, musical pitch.
words.example: The priest intoned the closing prayer in a steady, solemn voice that filled the chapel.
words.mnemonic: 'In tone' — you speak staying on one sustained musical tone.

words.definition: To repeat words rhythmically in a singing, monotonous way.
words.example: The crowd chanted the team's name over and over until the whole stadium shook.
words.mnemonic: It sits inside 'enchant' — repeated rhythmic words that cast a spell.

words.definition: To sing or hum softly and soothingly.
words.example: She crooned a lullaby, rocking gently, until the baby's eyes finally closed.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'swoon' — soft, tender singing that makes you melt.

words.definition: To shout in a deep, loud, powerful voice.
words.example: The sergeant bellowed his orders across the parade ground, and every recruit froze.
words.mnemonic: A raging 'bull below' the hill bellowing at full force.

words.definition: To cry out with a high, piercing, sharp sound.
words.example: She shrieked and jumped onto the chair when the spider dropped onto her shoulder.
words.mnemonic: Say it fast and it becomes the sharp 'eek!' it describes.

words.definition: To make a harsh, high-pitched, grating noise.
words.example: The tires screeched as the car braked hard and skidded around the corner.
words.mnemonic: The long 'eeee' grinds like the sound of brakes — screeeech.

words.definition: To make a loud, harsh cry like an alarmed bird.
words.example: The parrot squawked the instant the cat padded into the room.
words.mnemonic: The spelling looks like the sound a startled duck or parrot makes — 'kwawk!'

words.definition: To talk quickly and continuously about unimportant things.
words.example: The kids chattered nonstop about the amusement park for the entire bus ride home.
words.mnemonic: 'Chat' plus '-er', doubling on itself — endless, restless chatting.

words.definition: To talk casually about other people's private lives, often unkindly.
words.example: The neighbors gossiped for weeks about who had really bought the mansion on the corner.
words.mnemonic: 'Gos-SIP' your tea while you spill everyone's secrets.

words.definition: To reveal secret or private information to others.
words.example: The lawyer refused to divulge the whereabouts of her client under any pressure.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'di-BULGE' — a hidden secret bulging out until it bursts into the open.

words.definition: To reveal information that was previously kept secret or private.
words.example: The company refused to disclose how much its executives were paid.
words.mnemonic: dis-CLOSE — the opposite of keeping something closed; you open it up so others can see.

words.definition: To announce something publicly, officially, and with emphasis.
words.example: The king climbed to the balcony to proclaim victory to the cheering crowd.
words.mnemonic: PRO + CLAIM — you claim something PROudly and out loud for everyone to hear.

words.definition: To openly declare a feeling or belief, sometimes falsely.
words.example: He professed his undying loyalty, yet betrayed her the very next day.
words.mnemonic: Picture a PROFESSor standing at the podium, openly declaring what he believes.

words.definition: To argue or assert firmly that something is true.
words.example: The lawyer contended that the evidence had been planted by the police.
words.mnemonic: con-TEND — you TEND (defend) your side of an argument against the other person.

words.definition: To claim someone did something wrong, without yet offering proof.
words.example: Neighbors allege that the landlord ignored the broken heating all winter.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'a ledge' — an accusation resting on shaky, unproven ground.

words.definition: To protest or object forcefully to another person's actions or words.
words.example: She remonstrated with the referee after the obviously unfair penalty.
words.mnemonic: re-MONSTER-ate — you turn into a monster of protest when you strongly object.

words.definition: To express strong disagreement, urging someone to reconsider their behavior.
words.example: The teacher expostulated with the boy, begging him to stop cheating.
words.mnemonic: ex-POST-ulate — you POST a strong, reasoned objection out loud for someone to heed.

words.definition: To state a personal view or judgment about something.
words.example: The critic opined that the film was overlong and hopelessly dull.
words.mnemonic: OPINE has OPINION hiding inside it — to give one aloud.

words.definition: Expressing feelings or opinions in a loud and forceful way.
words.example: The vociferous crowd booed until the announcer left the stage.
words.mnemonic: VOICE-iferous — someone absolutely full of loud VOICE.

words.definition: Making a loud, confused noise or an insistent demand.
words.example: The clamorous fans pounded the doors, demanding to be let inside.
words.mnemonic: A CLAMOR is a noisy uproar — add -ous and you describe the noise itself.

words.definition: Loud and harsh-sounding in a way that grates unpleasantly.
words.example: Her strident voice cut through the meeting like a fire alarm.
words.mnemonic: A STRIDE-nt march has harsh, pounding footsteps — loud and jarring on the ears.

words.definition: High-pitched and piercing in sound, often unpleasantly so.
words.example: The child let out a shrill scream that made everyone wince.
words.mnemonic: SHRILL rhymes with 'drill' — both bore painfully into your ears.

words.definition: Loud, rough, and disorderly, especially from a rowdy group.
words.example: Raucous laughter spilled out of the bar late into the night.
words.mnemonic: RAUCOUS sounds like 'rowdy ruckus' — a loud, rough commotion.

words.definition: Producing a deep, full, and pleasingly rich sound.
words.example: The actor's sonorous voice filled the theater without any microphone.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'sonus' (sound) — think of a rich, resonant SONar ping.

words.definition: Sweet and soothing to hear, especially a gentle sound.
words.example: The dulcet notes of the lullaby soon sent the baby to sleep.
words.mnemonic: DULCET echoes 'dulce' (Spanish for sweet) — sweetness for the ears.

words.definition: Having a pleasant, tuneful quality that is agreeable to the ear.
words.example: Her melodious voice drifted through the hall, and the restless crowd fell quiet to listen.
words.mnemonic: MELODY + -ous — literally full of melody, like a song you want to hum.

words.definition: Combining to form a pleasing, consistent whole free of conflict.
words.example: The two founders ran such a harmonious partnership that staff never once heard them argue.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'harmony' + 'us' — when all of us are in harmony, things fit together.

words.definition: Clashing or disagreeing, especially in sound or opinion.
words.example: Against the calm strings, the trumpet's blaring entrance sounded jarring and discordant.
words.mnemonic: DIS- (apart) + CORD — strings or hearts pulled apart, out of tune.

words.definition: Producing a harsh, jarring combination of sounds that lack agreement.
words.example: The pianist struck a deliberately dissonant chord that made the audience wince.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'this ain't right' — dissonant notes just don't belong together.

words.definition: Understood or accepted without being openly stated.
words.example: By staying and saying nothing, she gave her tacit approval to the plan.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'tacere' (to be silent) — think music's 'tacet': stay silent, yet understood.

words.definition: Suggested or understood though not directly expressed.
words.example: There was an implicit warning in his tone, even though he never actually threatened anyone.
words.mnemonic: IN + PLICIT (fold, as in 'pleat') — the meaning is folded inside, not spoken aloud.

words.definition: Too great or overwhelming to be described in speech.
words.example: Standing at the canyon's rim, she felt an ineffable awe that no photograph could capture.
words.mnemonic: IN- (not) + EFF-able — you can't 'eff-ing' say it; words fail you.

words.definition: Unable to express oneself clearly in speech.
words.example: Grief left him inarticulate, and he could only manage a few broken, half-finished words.
words.mnemonic: IN- (not) + ARTICULATE — the joints of speech won't connect, so words won't join up.

words.definition: Confused and distorted so the meaning becomes unclear.
words.example: The voicemail was so garbled by static that we couldn't tell where to meet.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'gargled' — try talking while gargling water and your words come out jumbled.

words.definition: Not easily understood; hidden or vague in meaning.
words.example: The poem's ending is so obscure that critics still argue about what it means.
words.mnemonic: OB- (over) + SCURE (dark) — something covered in darkness is hard to make out.

words.definition: Very difficult to comprehend; requiring deep, specialized thought.
words.example: The lecture on quantum field theory grew so abstruse that half the room stopped taking notes.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'abstract' + 'obtuse' — ideas so abstract they feel obtuse and impenetrable.

words.definition: Overly elaborate and inflated in style, or swollen and bloated.
words.example: His report was so turgid, padded with grand phrases, that the point vanished under the flourishes.
words.mnemonic: Echoes 'turbid' and 'rigid' — swollen, stiff, bloated prose that's hard to wade through.

words.definition: Arrogantly self-important and full of exaggerated dignity.
words.example: The pompous host kept reminding everyone which prestigious schools his children attended.
words.mnemonic: Think 'pomp' and a puffed-up 'pom-pom' — all showy, inflated self-importance.

words.definition: An excess of words that adds little real meaning.
words.example: Strip away the verbiage and this ten-page memo could have been a single sentence.
words.mnemonic: VERB (word) + -age — a heap of words, like 'garbage' made entirely of language.

words.definition: The use of many roundabout words to avoid saying something directly.
words.example: Instead of admitting he was fired, he retreated into circumlocution about 'exploring new directions.'
words.mnemonic: CIRCUM (around) + LOCUTION (speech) — literally talking in circles around the point.
